### Game Theory in Cybersecurity: A Review of Applications, Models, and Challenges

Matthew Egan∗, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Mukesh Gautam†, Senior Member, IEEE, and Mohammed Ben-Idris∗, Senior Member, IEEE
∗Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan, USA †Electricity Infrastructure & Buildings Division, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, USA
Emails: eganmat2@msu.edu, mukesh.gautam@pnnl.gov, benidris@msu.edu
Abstract—There are no aspects of society left unchanged by the Internet. From commerce to communication, from entertainment to engineering, every industry and sphere of influence exists in a new state thanks to the advent of the information age. This convenience, rarely controverted, comes with capricious actors, who wish to gain access to these systems for myriad reasons, be it financial, political, or mere intellectual gain. This paper presents information that can help readers to better understand the fundamentals of cybersecurity from a game theory perspective, such as coalitional games, Colonel Blotto systems, or how to find Nash Equilibrium. This paper also reviews how game theory can enhance understanding of cybersecurity through cooperative and non-cooperative methods, such as information sharing, defense modeling, and attacker analysis. The authors use the analysis to serve as a bridge for those in either field who need a way to best comprehend the methodologies of their contrasting fields.
Index Terms—Colonel Blotto systems, Cybersecurity, Game Theory, Nash equilibrium.
I. INTRODUCTION
The Internet has become integral to daily life, creating nu-merous job opportunities and boosting the global economy [1]. However, increased reliance on digital systems has heightened susceptibility to cyber threats [2], which have grown with advanced communication technologies [3], [4]. The rising cost, frequency, and sophistication of cyber attacks highlight the need for robust cybersecurity measures. IBM’s 2023 report indicates the average cost of a data breach is USD 4.45 million, a 2.3% increase from 2022 and a 15.3% rise since 2020 [5]. Strengthening cybersecurity through innovative, proactive, and responsive strategies is now more crucial than ever.
In cybersecurity, various techniques have been proposed to enhance digital defenses. A Markov chain model in [6] ana-lyzes time resilience by optimizing security controls against multi-stage attacks within a budget. A mixed integer linear programming approach was introduced in [7] to optimize cybersecurity investments in supply chains, transforming a nonlinear model into a linear equivalent to select optimal safeguards and minimize costs. A two-stage stochastic pro-gramming model in [8] minimizes social costs in cybersecurity risk planning by balancing expenses and strategic attacker

actions. In [9], a networking topology design using multi-objective optimization and swarm intelligence was proposed to determine optimal sensor placement, with the black hole method performing best. For Internet of Everything (IoE) environments, the authors in [10] devised a strategy using portfolio management to minimize costs and maximize se-curity, demonstrating the effectiveness of robust optimization and NSGA-II in finding efficient solutions.
Despite numerous cybersecurity techniques such as opti-mization algorithms and advanced security protocols, evolving cyber threats continue to pose challenges. Game theory, with its focus on strategic interactions among rational agents, offers valuable insight to mitigate these threats. This paper reviews the application of both cooperative and non-cooperative game theory in cybersecurity, aiming to consolidate current knowl-edge and identify future research directions. Key contribu-tions include exploring game theory applications, introducing fundamental principles, assessing the effectiveness of non-cooperative models in understanding adversarial behavior, examining cooperative models for fostering collaboration, and discussing the challenges and future directions in applying game theory to cybersecurity.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Sec-tion II presents the overview of game theory and cybersecurity. The non-cooperative and cooperative game theory applications are discussed, respectively, in Section III and Section IV. Section V explores challenges and future direction of game theory application in cybersecurity. Lastly, Section VI provides concluding remarks.
II. CYBERSECURITY AND GAME THEORY FUNDAMENTALS
In this section, we delve into the fundamentals of both cy-bersecurity and game theory, providing an overview essential for understanding their intersection.
A. Cybersecurity
Cybersecurity is not just a technical concern but a critical element of modern warfare and national security. One of the main places where cybersecurity was most dramatically brought into reality was the 2014 invasion of Crimea by Russia, seen in [11], wherein part of Russian strategy in-volved the crippling of Ukrainian infrastructure and causing a blackout to prevent Ukrainian defenders from coordinating
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
against their advance. This is also viewable in the wider 2022 to present-day war between Ukraine and Russia, discussed in [12], wherein the networks of Ukraine were attacked in ways both physical through the damage and sabotage of infrastructure, and psychological, through statements such as a false call for surrender by Zelensky, or phishing attacks aimed at Ukrainian government and military accounts in order to gather intelligence for the Russian army. This can also apply on the battlefield itself, as jamming networks against drones on both sides are critical to prevent them from achieving small degrees of air superiority [13].
B. Game Theory and Types of Games
Game theory studies mathematical models of strategic in-teractions among rational agents, providing tools to assess complex interactions and rational behaviors in mutually in-teractive settings [14]. It helps to understand how defenders and attackers react to each other. These interactions can be represented by game theoretic models where each player aims to maximize their interests. In some scenarios, multiple players within an organization may collaborate to defend against cyber attacks, applying cooperative and non-cooperative game theoretical models.
Games in game theory are often analyzed through di-chotomies, such as coalitional versus non-coalitional games. In non-coalitional games, players compete individually to optimize their utility functions without forming alliances. In coalitional games, players form coalitions to optimize both individual and joint utilities; coalitions must provide equal or greater utilities than individual efforts [15]. Non-coalitional games focus on maximizing individual utilities, whereas coali-tional games aim to improve the coalition’s joint utility.
One notable example of game theory applied to cyber-security is the Colonel Blotto game [16]. In this game, an attacker and a defender allocate troops to $N$ bases, deciding where to attack or defend based on available resources. It lacks a pure Nash equilibrium, meaning no set of choices can improve payout for either player. This model is relevant to cybersecurity, particularly for brute force/DDoS attacks, where the attacker’s and defender’s energy levels are compared to secure a space. Fig. 1 visualizes this concept, highlighting the strategy of defending numerous distributed assets where attacking all resources at once offers no advantage, and opponents’ strategies are often unpredictable until enacted.
In a quantifiable game theory model, such as number of names leaked, or dollars lost, the payout or reward for each player is typically modeled as a set of matrices, where any distinct strategy will give a distinct reward, as displayed in Eq. (1) for a two-player game with players a and b with a set of X and Y choices, respectively. These are often represented by arbitrary numbers or integers, but they represent real world choices that can have serious consequences, as the choice between doing nothing for data security is steep enough to warrant studies as deep as this, and far deeper still. For instance, in Colonel Blotto games such as [16], the reward

C. Deception
Deception is a common tactic in cybersecurity used by both attackers and defenders. Reference [17] provides exam-ples such as honey-potting, obfuscation, and moving target defenses. Some obfuscation methods are intuitive for average users, like falsely naming files, distributing databases across multiple servers, or storing data on external hard drives to make it difficult for attackers to locate. The book [17] draws an analogy from [18], describing how animals evolve bright markings as a method of deception to deter predators, known as mimesis or mimicry. Conversely, animals may use crypsis to make the truth more cryptic. In game theory, these methods prevent one side from gaining complete information, thereby hindering their decision-making processes.
This lack of information would make game theory difficult to fully implement as a strategy, as a rewards matrix would rely upon data such as likelihood of success or a reasonable expec-tation of the opponent’s strategies, but can be inferred from information available, such as public reports of hacking, or probes into one’s own systems for vulnerabilities. For instance, if one were to utilize honey-potting, as done in [17], they can determine how an attacker would breach their defenses, so even if they fail to capture the identity of the one who hacked them, they can look into their own logs, see what the strategy to breach their systems was, and implement IT patches to prevent further break-ins. Dedicating resources to this form of deception allows one to gain data without “winning”, or at least appearing to lose.
III. NON-COOPERATIVE GAME THEORY IN CYBERSECURITY
Cybersecurity is best modeled through the lens of attackers and defenders with incomplete information. This is because the main way that cybersecurity interactions occur is through hackers (attackers) attempting to secure resources from places
like data centers, banks, or as a means to disrupt the business operations of a company.
A. Attacker Modeling
The paper [19] describes attackers by sub-groups, helping defenders allocate resources effectively. Although written from the perspective of an electric grid operator defending substa-tions, its approach is generalizable. Attackers are modeled through six categories to determine cost, plus one for in-tent: knowledge, financial support, manpower, determination, stealthiness, expertise, and intended impact. These categories reflect how much a group values specific traits. For instance, nation-states prioritize stealthiness to avoid jeopardizing their standing, while “hacktivists” or terrorists may struggle with financial support or expertise but might not prioritize stealth.
The intended impact helps assess the likelihood of an attack. A terrorist is unlikely to target small business PCs due to low political gain, whereas a cybercriminal might find extortion more feasible. Conversely, the risk of a cybercriminal attacking a military base is low due to life-threatening repercussions and minimal payout. However, a state actor might target such a base during wartime, as the potential consequences are already maximized by existing hostilities. This nuanced understanding of attackers aids in developing targeted and effective defense strategies.
B. Defender Modeling
The National Electrical Reliability Corporation Critical In-frastructure Protection (NERC-CIP) [20] is a standard for evaluating network security, established by the National En-ergy Regulatory Committee in the US to ensure consistent electricity supply. It uses six categories to evaluate the security of each network: personnel and training, electronic security perimeter, physical security, system security management, recovery plans for cyber systems, and information protection. The paper describing NERC grades each category from 0 to 3 based on investment and implementation time. This holistic approach may not capture all defense nuances; for instance, perfect backup systems are useful but can disrupt operations if overused, and secure bases are ineffective if protected by default passwords.
In a game theory context, these scores determine the “hard-ness” for attackers, indicating the cost of attacking from differ-ent angles. Systems with weak training are more vulnerable to phishing, and public access to unsecured rooms makes attacks easier.
C. Nash Equilibrium in Cybersecurity
Nash Equilibrium in cybersecurity varies depending on whether the context is attacking or defending. For example, in a zero-sum game, the goal might be to maximize damage or minimize costs, influenced by available resources. In [21], the authors discuss a multi-stage, zero-sum game model for cybersecurity in cyber-physical systems. They illustrate that limited attacker resources force a focus on the easiest targets, assessing target value based on intrinsic monetary worth and
network connections. A more connected switch is more valu-able than one with fewer connections. In cybersecurity, Nash Equilibrium is reached when both attackers and defenders play rationally and cannot improve their positions without the other’s cooperation, representing the “safest” option. In [21], this equilibrium is achieved iteratively, with repeated attack and defense cycles until neither side can gain new information, effectively solving the game.
Nash equilibrium is stated in logical terms by Eq. (2). It shows the mathematics behind a system, where the payout P for attacker a for a strategy i, or for defender d for a strategy j. Neither player can unilaterally alter the course of their decision making without coming to a worse outcome. They would need to force the other player to come to a different decision, or find some alternate outcome ahead of time that would be ideal for both parties, which would be irrational in an adversarial, atomized model of a particular game model.

IV. COOPERATIVE GAME THEORY IN CYBERSECURITY
The application of cooperative game theory to cybersecurity is explored in this section, focusing on how collaboration between different entities can enhance security measures.
A. Cooperative Game Models for Collaboration
Cooperative game models are pivotal for fostering collabo-ration among different entities or organizations in cybersecu-rity [22]. These models enable stakeholders to work together, sharing resources and information to enhance their collective security posture. A cooperative game model for rewarding and participation-fee allocation in cybersecurity information exchange has been presented in [23], where cooperative game models were used to encourage collaboration and information sharing among organizations. [24] investigates the ideals of cooperation among different divisions within an organization with dependent security assets. It also studies vulnerabilities that increase security risks, and formulates a game model of cooperation possibilities amongst these divisions based on their synergistic and incongruous interdependencies.
B. Cooperative Solution Approaches in Cybersecurity
Solution approaches in cooperative game theory, such as the Shapley value and the Nucleolus, play an important role in allocating resources fairly among acknowledged stakeholders. The Shapley value is a solution concept that assigns a value to each player based on their contribution to the success of the coalition [25]. It helps quantify the contributions of different entities, ensuring equitable distribution of resources such as funding, personnel, and technology. In [26], a Shapley value distribution mechanism for cyber threat intelligence sharing among organizations is proposed, where intelligence sharing was modeled as a cooperative game. Players could share intelligence and gain from of reduced risk of cyber attacks. The Shapley value solution approach from cooperative game theory was used to fairly distribute the benefits (reduced risk) among the organizations in a coalition based on their
contributions, where the concept of a “risk coefficient” was introduced to account for the varying levels of risk faced by different organizations [26].
The Nucleolus, another popular solution concept, focuses on maximizing the maximum dissatisfaction among players, providing a stable and fair allocation of resources. The Nucle-olus solution approach was used in [27] to address strategic subchannel resource allocation in a wireless mesh networks (WMNs). The applicability of the Nucleolus solution was highlighted in providing a strategic interference management approach by allocating subchannels to mesh routers based on their interference levels with neighbors, while ensuring a fair and efficient distribution of resources [27].
C. Collaborative Cybersecurity Strategies
Collaborative cybersecurity strategies are essential for ad-dressing the complex and evolving landscape of cyber threats. Cooperative game theory provides a framework for develop-ing and implementing these strategies, enabling entities to work together more effectively. The need for international collaboration and coordination in developing a global legal framework for cybersecurity, particularly for protecting critical infrastructure, has been highlighted in [28], where the authors suggest using cooperative game theory to establish incentives for nations to strengthen their cybersecurity laws.
One of the best and most common forms of cybersecurity defenses is to share information amongst firms. This is a low-cost way to prevent data breaches, and an effective way to prevent hacks. If you know one firm was harmed by a phishing email, and you can see exactly the form it took, then you can flag that, and ensure that it is moved automatically to spam if an identical email is sent to your employees. Likewise, and on a more intricate level, if you find the IP of a hacker, then you can ensure that any subsequent hacks are more quickly traced and reported if they harm someone you have collaborated with. These are just two of the myriad ways that one can form a more effective strategy at low cost, and build trust amongst industry partners.
V. CHALLENGES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
In this section, we identify the key challenges faced in applying game theory to cybersecurity and outline potential directions for future research.
A. Challenges in Applying Game Theory to Cybersecurity
Applying game theory to cybersecurity, while promising, presents several challenges that need to be addressed to fully harness its potential. Some of the key challenges are briefly discussed below.

1. Complexity and Scalability: One of the primary chal-lenges is the complexity and scalability of game-theoretic models. Cybersecurity scenarios often involve numerous play-ers, each with diverse strategies and objectives. Modeling these scenarios accurately can lead to highly complex mathematical formulations that are difficult to solve, especially as the number of participants grows. Developing scalable algorithms
   that can handle large-scale cybersecurity problems remains a critical area of research [29].
2. Dynamic and Evolving Threat Landscape: The dynamic and evolving nature of cyber threats adds another layer of complexity. Game-theoretic models typically assume static en-vironments, but cyber threats continuously change and adapt. Incorporating this dynamism into game-theoretic models is essential for their practical application. Researchers need to develop adaptive game-theoretic frameworks that can respond to the changing threat landscape in real time [29].
3. Data Availability and Quality: The effectiveness of game-theoretic models heavily relies on the availability and quality of data. Accurate data on cyber threats, vulnerabilities, and the behaviors of different actors are crucial for building reliable models [30]. However, obtaining such data is chal-lenging due to privacy concerns, data sharing restrictions, and the often-sensitive nature of cybersecurity information [31]. Ensuring data integrity and overcoming data-sharing barriers are significant hurdles that need to be addressed.
4. Interdisciplinary Collaboration: Cybersecurity is inher-ently interdisciplinary, involving aspects of computer science, information technology, psychology, economics, and more. Effective application of game theory to cybersecurity requires collaboration across these disciplines [32]. Bridging the gap between theoretical game-theoretic research and practical cy-bersecurity implementation demands cooperation among re-searchers, practitioners, and policymakers.
   B. Future Directions
   Despite challenges, the potential benefits of applying game theory to cybersecurity are immense. Several future directions can advance this field:
5. Real-time and Adaptive Game Theory: Future research should focus on creating real-time and adaptive game-theoretic frameworks that can respond to the evolving cyber threat landscape. This involves developing algorithms that can update strategies based on new information and changing conditions, ensuring that cybersecurity measures remain effective against emerging threats [33].
6. Improved Data Sharing and Collaboration: Enhancing data sharing and collaboration among different entities is cru-cial for the success of game-theoretic models in cybersecurity. Establishing secure and trusted platforms for sharing threat intelligence and cybersecurity data can significantly improve the quality of game-theoretic models. Encouraging interdisci-plinary collaboration can also lead to more comprehensive and effective solutions.
7. Policy and Regulatory Support: Support from policy-makers and regulatory bodies is essential to address the challenges related to data sharing and interdisciplinary col-laboration. Developing policies that incentivize data sharing while protecting privacy and encouraging collaboration across different sectors can facilitate the application of game theory to cybersecurity.
8. Case Studies and Practical Implementation: Conducting more case studies and practical implementations of game-theoretic models in real-world cybersecurity scenarios can provide valuable insights and validate theoretical research. These case studies can help identify practical challenges and refine theoretical models, bridging the gap between research and practice.
   VI. CONCLUSION
   Cybersecurity can stand to benefit greatly from greater consideration of the use of game theory. Game theory, as a realm of study, benefits those fields most that rely upon determining how to best either cooperate with others, or to predict other actors in realms of incomplete information. This matches closely with how one can comprehend the field of cybersecurity, both in how to best share information with others amid privacy and competing business concerns, and in more adversarial contexts. From the realms of data breaches to training time, laying out strategies are always made more effective when they come alongside rigorous and rational planning. This paper has helped to serve as an overview of the applicability of game theory. Those who have read this paper will come away with enough of an understanding of how it has already been applied, and how it can be applied to their own methods of cybersecurity. In any event, once one systematizes these realms, the benefits of combining these realms can become far more apparent.
